9.2 — Hex, RGB & Data Abstraction

You have clicked colors in Unity a hundred times. Behind that picker is the exact place where binary becomes USEFUL: colors are bytes, written in hex, and the hex is just binary with better handwriting. Today you read the Inspector's secret language.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I read a colour as a number?”
Break It Down~10 min

Read one colour out of your own game — from the swatch in the Inspector, down to the four bytes it is really made of, and back again — without a converter open.

First, before anything else: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Cut the hex string into byteswhat does this part do?Read: the Dec/Hex/Bin table in this lesson's Concept Lab, and the hex section of Binary & Hex
  2. Read one byte as a channel valuewhat does this part do?Read: the eight-bits-stop-at-255 rule from 9.1, read against the same table
  3. Say what the fourth byte iswhat does this part do?Read: the Color32 paragraph of the Binary & Hex reference
  4. Count what the channels can expresswhat does this part do?Read: the colour-count socratic in this lesson's Concept Lab, argued from 9.1's bits-to-range law
  5. Put the colour somewhere you can change it oncewhat does this part do?Read: Step 2 of the Build Lab below, and the palette class it builds

The split is the whole lesson. "What colour is #FFE681?" is one question, and with a converter open it is a lookup; these five are five moves you can make on paper, and the last one is the move the exam grades as abstraction. A colour is not a picture and not a name — it is four numbers you chose, each with a range somebody else fixed at 0 to 255, and every colour bug in this unit is one of those four numbers being something you did not expect.

The test: could you decode a colour with a pencil and the table on this page? If a step needs the eyedropper open, it is not part of reading a colour — it is part of finding one.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The coin you collect is drawn from Coin_Animation.png, whose busiest colour is #FFE681. Write it as three decimal bytes, then as a Color32 call — and say which of those two spellings you would rather review in somebody else's code, and why.

All three scenes in this project have the same camera background — the float triple (0.192, 0.302, 0.475) — because nobody ever changed Unity's default. Convert it to bytes, then to hex, then say which struct the scene file is actually storing and what changes if you move it into a Color32.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Hex = binary in groups of 4. One hex digit (0–9, A–F) covers exactly 4 bits: 0000=0 … 1111=F. A byte is therefore exactly TWO hex digits. Nobody reads 1111111111111111 when FF FF says the same thing out loud.

Dec0123456789101112131415
Hex0123456789ABCDEF
Bin0000000100100011010001010110011110001001101010111100110111101111

A color is four bytes. Unity's Color32 is R, G, B, A — one byte each, 0–255, so a color is literally a hex number like FFE681FF (full red, a strong green, a little blue, full alpha). When you type new Color32(255, 230, 129, 255) you are writing FFE681FF in decimal cosplay. Here are three colours from your own project and from this page, decoded by hand:

// The coin you collect is drawn from Coin_Animation.png.
// Its busiest colour is #FFE681 → R=ff=255, G=e6=230, B=81=129

// The site you are reading right now is themed blue:
// #6cb2ff → R=6c=108, G=b2=178, B=ff=255  → (108, 178, 255)

// All three of your scenes still carry Unity's default camera
// background, because nobody ever chose anything else:
// (0.192, 0.302, 0.475) as floats → (49, 77, 121) as bytes → #314D79

That last one is worth a second look. The camera shows you a Color — four floats between 0 and 1 — and the machine's idea of the same colour is three bytes. Multiply each float by 255 and round: 0.192 × 255 = 49, which is 0x31. Same colour, two spellings, and the byte one is the one you can count with. The # in CSS means "hex follows," and web colors are 6 hex digits because web alpha is written separately.

Socratic

The exam loves this: "how many colors can RGB represent?" Work it — 256 per channel, three channels — and say WHY the answer is 256³ (that is 9.1's bits-to-range law, cubed). Then: why is 4 bits per channel (like old consoles) only 4096 colors — what did 8-bit color BUY?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — decode your game's palette. Every Sprite Renderer in this project is still on its default tint — (1, 1, 1, 1), which is #FFFFFF — so no object in the game is tinted from code. What you see on screen is the artwork and nothing else, which means the art IS the palette. Read three colours out of it with an eyedropper (the Sprite Editor has one, and so does any image editor), and write the hex AND the decimal triple for each:

  • the stone ground tileset your cave walls are cut from — a desaturated grey
  • the coin sheet, Coin_Animation.png — a bright gold
  • the blood on the axe blade — a very dark red
Check your answers write both spellings first

Then compare. Each hex pair is one byte and each byte is a decimal number from 0 to 255, so this is three conversions per colour, not nine.

  • stone: #878579 = (135, 133, 121)
  • coin gold: #FFE681 = (255, 230, 129)
  • axe blood: #8A2000 = (138, 32, 0)

Then pick a fourth colour of your own and do the same. Notice what the hex made visible in one glance: the stone is high in all three channels and low in saturation, the gold is high in R and G with almost no B, and the blood is almost all R. Now you can QUOTE that instead of gesturing at it.

Step 2 — program a palette. Colors as data — the abstraction, in code. These are the three you just read, with the byte values the eyedropper gave you:

public static class Palette
{
    //              what the eyedropper found    hex        Color32
    public static readonly Color32 CAVE_ROCK = new Color32(0x87, 0x85, 0x79, 0xff);
    public static readonly Color32 COIN_GOLD = new Color32(0xff, 0xe6, 0x81, 0xff);
    public static readonly Color32 BLOOD     = new Color32(0x8a, 0x20, 0x00, 0xff);
}

// the hit flash 8.3 asks you to build, written out:
spriteRenderer.color = new Color32(0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff); // white for 0.1s
// phase 3 boss tint:
spriteRenderer.color = Palette.BLOOD;

Why a palette class beats per-object color picking: change ONE line, the whole game's mood shifts — and every object that was reading it changes at the same time, with no object-by-object hunting. That is abstraction — the exam's word, in your repo. It is also the reason the numbers above had to be read off the art rather than guessed: a palette is only worth anything if it is the same colour the artist drew.

Step 3 — the alpha byte. The fourth byte is transparency. 0xff = solid; 0x80 = half-visible (the hit flash above could EASE from 0x80 to 0xff instead of snapping). Every prefab in this project is currently #FFFFFFFF — fully opaque — so pick one and change only the fourth byte. Turret_Projectile.prefab is the clearest to watch: it draws Turret_Bullet.png, whose busiest colour is #008DF0, and dropping its alpha to 0x80 turns that solid blue bullet into a suggestion of one. Note the readability change: transparent threats read as "avoidable" — alpha is communication, not decoration.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Convert hex ↔ binary ↔ decimal for bytes, fast
  • Explain a color as four bytes and decode #RRGGBB by hand
  • Build a palette class as a data abstraction
  • Do the 256³ color-count argument from bits
  • Break "read a colour as a number" into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part came from, and where you would reread it
